claim: Aquaporin (AQP) channels facilitate passive water transport across cell membranes.
source: Aquaporin (AQP) channels facillitate passive water transport across cell membranes (Preston et al., 1992; Li and Wang, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Preston et al., 1992 and Li and Wang, 2017.

claim: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels are highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet that ensheath the cerebral vasculature.
source: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels are highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet that ensheath the cerebral vasculature (Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013), covering up to 20–60% of the perivascular endfeet membrane facing the vessel wall (Nielsen et al., 1997; Wolburg et al., 2011; Rash et al., 1998; Rasmussen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013; Nielsen et al., 1997; Wolburg et al., 2011; Rash et al., 1998; Rasmussen et al., 2022.

claim: AQP4 covers up to 20–60% of the perivascular endfeet membrane facing the vessel wall.
source: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels are highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet that ensheath the cerebral vasculature (Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013), covering up to 20–60% of the perivascular endfeet membrane facing the vessel wall (Nielsen et al., 1997; Wolburg et al., 2011; Rash et al., 1998; Rasmussen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nielsen et al., 1997; Wolburg et al., 2011; Rash et al., 1998; Rasmussen et al., 2022.

claim: Brain endothelial cells are essentially devoid of the AQP1 water channels expressed by endothelial cells in peripheral tissues.
source: This high density of water channels in astrocytic vascular endfeet is remarkable because brain endothelial cells are essentially devoid of the AQP1 water channels expressed by endothelial cells in peripheral tissues (Bonomini and Rezzani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bonomini and Rezzani, 2010.

claim: Genetic deletion of AQP4 in mice results in an increased brain water content.
source: Genetic deletion of AQP4 (AQP4 KO) in mice results in an increased brain water content (Katada et al., 2014; Li et al., 2009), an expanded interstitial fluid (ISF) volume fraction (Katada et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2008), decreased ventricular volume (Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Li et al., 2009), and decreased capacity to buffer interstitial potassium (K+) ions (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Strohschein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Katada et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2009.

claim: Genetic deletion of AQP4 in mice results in an expanded interstitial fluid (ISF) volume fraction.
source: Genetic deletion of AQP4 (AQP4 KO) in mice results in an increased brain water content (Katada et al., 2014; Li et al., 2009), an expanded interstitial fluid (ISF) volume fraction (Katada et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2008), decreased ventricular volume (Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Li et al., 2009), and decreased capacity to buffer interstitial potassium (K+) ions (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Strohschein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Katada et al., 2014 and Yao et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic deletion of AQP4 in mice results in decreased ventricular volume.
source: Genetic deletion of AQP4 (AQP4 KO) in mice results in an increased brain water content (Katada et al., 2014; Li et al., 2009), an expanded interstitial fluid (ISF) volume fraction (Katada et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2008), decreased ventricular volume (Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Li et al., 2009), and decreased capacity to buffer interstitial potassium (K+) ions (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Strohschein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2009.

claim: Genetic deletion of AQP4 in mice results in decreased capacity to buffer interstitial potassium (K+) ions.
source: Genetic deletion of AQP4 (AQP4 KO) in mice results in an increased brain water content (Katada et al., 2014; Li et al., 2009), an expanded interstitial fluid (ISF) volume fraction (Katada et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2008), decreased ventricular volume (Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Li et al., 2009), and decreased capacity to buffer interstitial potassium (K+) ions (Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Strohschein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b and Strohschein et al., 2011.

claim: The glymphatic system is comprised of a network of annular perivascular spaces formed by astrocytic endfeet ensheathing the vascular walls.
source: The glymphatic system is comprised of a network of annular perivascular spaces formed by astrocytic endfeet ensheathing the vascular walls.
evidence: The claim is stated in the manuscript text and is based on established knowledge of the glymphatic system.

claim: Perivascular spaces form a low resistance pathway enabling cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and ISF exchange, promoting the clearance of interstitial solutes from the brain.
source: Perivascular spaces form a low resistance pathway enabling cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and ISF exchange, promoting the clearance of interstitial solutes from the brain (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iliff et al., 2012.

claim: AQP4 KO mice exhibit a 25–60% decrease in glymphatic CSF tracer influx.
source: AQP4 KO mice exhibit a 25–60% decrease in glymphatic CSF tracer influx (Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019), and acute pharmacological blockade of AQP4 inhibits glymphatic transport using TGN-020 inhibitor (Huber et al., 2009; Harrison et al., 2020; Takano and Yamada, 2020), reducing severity of brain edema and lesion volume after ischemic injury (Igarashi et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Acute pharmacological blockade of AQP4 using TGN-020 inhibitor inhibits glymphatic transport.
source: AQP4 KO mice exhibit a 25–60% decrease in glymphatic CSF tracer influx (Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019), and acute pharmacological blockade of AQP4 inhibits glymphatic transport using TGN-020 inhibitor (Huber et al., 2009; Harrison et al., 2020; Takano and Yamada, 2020), reducing severity of brain edema and lesion volume after ischemic injury (Igarashi et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huber et al., 2009; Harrison et al., 2020; Takano and Yamada, 2020.

claim: TGN-020 inhibitor reduces severity of brain edema and lesion volume after ischemic injury.
source: AQP4 KO mice exhibit a 25–60% decrease in glymphatic CSF tracer influx (Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019), and acute pharmacological blockade of AQP4 inhibits glymphatic transport using TGN-020 inhibitor (Huber et al., 2009; Harrison et al., 2020; Takano and Yamada, 2020), reducing severity of brain edema and lesion volume after ischemic injury (Igarashi et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Igarashi et al., 2011 and Sun et al., 2022.

claim: In cell-based assays TGN-020 inhibitor failed to inhibit AQP4.
source: However, in cell-based assays TGN-020 inhibitor failed to inhibit AQP4, bringing into question the true molecular mechanisms of its action (Verkman et al., 2017), discussed in Choi et al., 2021.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verkman et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of AQP4 accelerates buildup of neurotoxic protein waste in neurodegenerative models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Deletion of AQP4 also accelerates buildup of neurotoxic protein waste in neurodegenerative models of Alzheimer's (Xu et al., 2015; Ishida et al., 2022) and Parkinson's disease (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2015 and Ishida et al., 2022.

claim: Deletion of AQP4 accelerates buildup of neurotoxic protein waste in neurodegenerative models of Parkinson's disease.
source: Deletion of AQP4 also accelerates buildup of neurotoxic protein waste in neurodegenerative models of Alzheimer's (Xu et al., 2015; Ishida et al., 2022) and Parkinson's disease (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cui et al., 2021.

claim: A common single nucleotide AQP4 polymorphism is correlated to changes in slow-wave non-REM sleep and cognition in humans.
source: In humans, a common single nucleotide AQP4 polymorphism is correlated to changes in slow-wave non-REM sleep and cognition (Ulv Larsen et al., 2020), consistent with increased glymphatic function during sleep (Xie et al., 2013; Eide et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ulv Larsen et al., 2020.

claim: Glymphatic function is increased during sleep.
source: In humans, a common single nucleotide AQP4 polymorphism is correlated to changes in slow-wave non-REM sleep and cognition (Ulv Larsen et al., 2020), consistent with increased glymphatic function during sleep (Xie et al., 2013; Eide et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xie et al., 2013 and Eide et al., 2021.

claim: Vascular polarized AQP4 expression in the astrocytic vascular endfeet is functionally crucial for fluid transport.
source: Thus, the evidence suggests that it is the vascular polarized AQP4 expression in the astrocytic vascular endfeet functionally crucial for fluid transport, and not necessarily total AQP4 levels in the tissue (Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Sylvain et al., 2021; Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003a; Eide and Hansson, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mestre et al., 2018a; Hablitz et al., 2020; Sylvain et al., 2021; Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003a; Eide and Hansson, 2018.

claim: AQP4 KO mice had brain volumes 5–10% larger than wildtype mice.
source: We found the brain volume 5–10% larger in AQP4 KO than in WT mice (p<0.01, mean ± SD KO = 521 ± 13 vs. WT = 477 ± 24 mm3; Figure 1A) with no significant differences between animal age (p=0.697), body weight (p=0.7662) or signal-to-noise ratio (p=0.1385) of the 3D-CISS images from two genotypes (Table 1– Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AQP4 KO mice had ~6% increase in brain water content measured ex vivo compared to wildtype mice.
source: This difference in brain volume coincided with ~6% increase in the brain water content measured ex vivo (p<0.05, min-max of 2–11%, KO = 3.66 ± 0.09 vs. WT = 3.46 ± 0.05 ml/g dry brain weight; Figure 1D; Li et al., 2009; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1D, with additional citations to Li et al., 2009 and Haj-Yasein et al., 2011.

claim: Total CSF volume was estimated as 2.4–4.4% of the parenchymal volume among all animals.
source: Total CSF volume was estimated as 2.4–4.4% of the parenchymal volume among all animals and no difference in delineated CSF space volumes was found between KO and WT (p=0.1255, KO = 15.1 ± 1.9 vs. WT = 17.7 ± 2.4 mm3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No difference in delineated CSF space volumes was found between AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: Total CSF volume was estimated as 2.4–4.4% of the parenchymal volume among all animals and no difference in delineated CSF space volumes was found between KO and WT (p=0.1255, KO = 15.1 ± 1.9 vs. WT = 17.7 ± 2.4 mm3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The whole segmented CSF space to brain volume ratio was 23–29% smaller in AQP4 KO compared to wildtype mice.
source: Yet the whole segmented CSF space to brain volume ratio was 23–29% smaller in KO compared to WT (p<0.05, KO = 2.99 ± 0.43 % vs. WT = 3.86 ± 0.41 %; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The difference in CSF space to brain volume ratio was mainly noted within the ventricular system comprising of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles.
source: This difference was mainly noted within the ventricular system comprising of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles (p<0.05; Figure 1C), consistent with previous ex vivo (Li et al., 2009) or lower resolution 2D assessment with low-field strength MRI (Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Trillo-Contreras et al., 2021; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C, with additional citations to Li et al., 2009; Trillo-Contreras et al., 2018; Trillo-Contreras et al., 2021.

claim: Similar CSF volume production was found in AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: These changes in the ventricular volume were not driven by CSF production, since we found similar CSF volume production in AQP4 KO and WT mice (Figure 1E) using a newly developed in vivo approach (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1E, with citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: No differences were noted in the segmented perivascular CSF space between AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: Perhaps most surprisingly, no differences were noted in the segmented perivascular CSF space between KO and WT (p=0.1623; Figure 1C) or its individual components (skull base/ Circle of Willis, p=0.9307; basilar artery, p=0.4286; anterior/posterior perivascular spaces, p=0.2486; Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C and Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: Both awake and ketamine/xylazine anesthetized AQP4 KO mice exhibited a larger interstitial space compared to wildtype mice.
source: Quantification of interstitial space volume using real-time iontophoresis with tetramethylammonium (TMA) (Odackal et al., 2017), showed that both awake and ketamine/xylazine anesthetized AQP4 KO mice exhibited a larger interstitial space (p<0.05 for both, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1F, with citation to Odackal et al., 2017.

claim: No difference in tortuosity was found between AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: We found no difference in tortuosity between genotypes (p=0.1412, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ADC and D (IVIM) provided similar results.
source: ADC and D (IVIM) provided similar results (Pearson's linear correlation, r=0.94, P<0.0001, Appendix 1—figure 1B), and no differences were found within all 5 large CSF space regions (Table 2, Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Appendix 1—figure 1B.

claim: AQP4 KO animals exhibited ADC and D 5.7 ± 1.5 % higher than in wildtype mice.
source: Both revealed increased slow diffusion measures within the brain parenchyma, with KO animals exhibiting ADC and D 5.7 ± 1.5 % higher than in WT (Figure 2A and C), consistent with previous ADC estimates in KO animals using lower resolution at 7 Tesla MR and time-dependent diffusion (Pavlin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2A and C, with citation to Pavlin et al., 2017.

claim: No difference in average D*, Fp and the product of Fp × D* was found within all parenchymal regions from AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: We found no differences in average D*, Fp and the product of Fp × D* within all parenchymal regions from KO and WT mice (Table 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Table 2A.

claim: No significant differences in the vascular density were found between AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: This suggests similar blood perfusion, and is supported with our histological analysis showing no significant differences in the vascular density between the genotypes (Figure 2F), with a trend towards a small increase within the thalamus and olfactory bulb (11 and 15 %, respectively; both p≈0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The peak and overall magnitude of the parenchymal signal enhancement were significantly lower in AQP4 KO than wildtype brains.
source: Yet, the peak and overall magnitude of the parenchymal signal enhancement were significantly lower in KO than WT brains (lowest p<0.01; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: AQP4 KO mice exhibited substantially less tracer accumulation around the venous sinuses compared to wildtype mice.
source: Finally, while the tracer in WT accumulated around the venous sinuses as previously reported (Iliff et al., 2013), the AQP4 KO mice exhibited substantially less accumulation (p=0.0148; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3D, with citation to Iliff et al., 2013.

claim: The arrival time of tracer was similar, if slightly longer in AQP4 KO than in wildtype mice.
source: Overall, the arrival time was similar, if slightly longer in KO than in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The duration of time-to-peak was ~30% longer in AQP4 KO among all regions.
source: The duration of time-to-peak was ~30% longer in KO among all regions, with the largest difference visible in the hippocampus, midbrain, thalamus, cerebellum and superior sagittal sinus, though this trend was not significant due to high variability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The area under the DCE curve consistently was smaller in AQP4 KO mice.
source: This would be confirmed with the area under the DCE curve that consistently was smaller in KO (Table 3, 'Mean AUC').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Table 3.

claim: Vascular density did not correlate with ADC or IVIM measures in both AQP4 KO and wildtype animals.
source: The vascular density did not correlate with ADC or IVIM measures in both KO and WT animals (Figure 2G, Appendix 1—figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2G and Appendix 1—figure 1D.

claim: In wildtype mice, AQP4 expression had a moderate linear correlation with both ADC and D.
source: Interestingly, in WT mice AQP4 expression did not correlate with changes in the MR tracer dynamics (Appendix 1—figure 2D), but had a moderate linear correlation with both ADC (r=0.77, p=0.0092) and D (r=0.74, p=0.0137; Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: There was no correlation found between the vascular density and AQP4 expression.
source: Finally, there was no correlation found between the vascular density and AQP4 expression (both Pearson's and Spearman's correlation absolute value <0.52 and p>0.16), or between MR diffusion and tracer dynamics parameters (correlation value <0.5 and p>0.05 for any comparison) except for low correlation between the area under the DCE curve and ADC for both genotypes (WT: r=0.63, p=0.0272; KO: r=0.64, p=0.0239).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: High vascular density predicts fast CSF tracer influx.
source: Thus, high vascular density predicts fast CSF tracer influx consistent with the notion that CSF is pumped in along the perivascular spaces surrounding arteries (Iliff et al., 2012; Iliff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Iliff et al., 2012 and Iliff et al., 2013.

claim: The markedly altered brain fluid transport in AQP4 KO mice may result from a reduction in glymphatic fluid export, leading to stagnation of ISF and enlargement of the interstitial space.
source: Thus, our data overall suggest that the markedly altered brain fluid transport in AQP4 KO mice may result from a reduction in glymphatic fluid export, leading to stagnation of ISF and enlargement of the interstitial space.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The interstitial fluid stagnation will reduce CSF influx and give rise to an overall reduction in glymphatic transport.
source: The interstitial fluid stagnation will in turn reduce CSF influx and give rise to an overall reduction in glymphatic transport.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AQPs increase membrane water permeability and are present in kidney and exocrine organs where fluid transport is driven by relatively small osmotic gradients produced by plasma membrane ion transporters.
source: In general, AQPs increase membrane water permeability and are present in kidney and exocrine organs where fluid transport is driven by relatively small osmotic gradients produced by plasma membrane ion transporters (Salman et al., 2022; Salman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salman et al., 2022 and Salman et al., 2021.

claim: AQPs facilitate near-isomolar transepithelial fluid transport.
source: AQPs facilitate near-isomolar transepithelial fluid transport and AQP deletions have previously been shown to be associated with reduced fluid secretion (Verkman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verkman, 2009.

claim: AQP deletions have been shown to be associated with reduced fluid secretion.
source: AQPs facilitate near-isomolar transepithelial fluid transport and AQP deletions have previously been shown to be associated with reduced fluid secretion (Verkman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verkman, 2009.

claim: AQP4 sharply reduces outflow of interstitial fluid.
source: A recent study showed that AQP4 sharply reduces outflow of interstitial fluid (Plá et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Plá et al., 2022.

claim: Brain interstitial fluid leaves by multiple pathways including perivenous efflux, along cranial and spinal nerves and also along the ventricular and pial surfaces.
source: It has been shown that brain interstitial fluid leaves by multiple pathways including perivenous efflux, along cranial and spinal nerves and also along the ventricular and pial surfaces (Rasmussen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rasmussen et al., 2022.

claim: AQP4 is intensely expressed in glia limitans facing the ependymal layers of the ventricles and also the pial membrane surrounding the brain surfaces.
source: AQP4 is intensely expressed in glia limitans facing the ependymal layers of the ventricles and also the pial membrane surrounding the brain surfaces.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of AQP4 expression.

claim: Recent studies showed dynamic and reversible AQP4 channel membrane relocalization for regulation of local water homeostasis.
source: Recent studies showed dynamic and reversible AQP4 channel membrane relocalization for regulation of local water homeostasis (Salman et al., 2022) in response to hypothermia and hypotonic treatment in cultured rat (Kitchen et al., 2015) and human primary cortical astrocytes (Salman et al., 2017) without change in AQP4 mRNA levels, and nonuniformity of these responses among AQP4 subtypes (Ciappelloni et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salman et al., 2022; Kitchen et al., 2015; Salman et al., 2017; Ciappelloni et al., 2019.

claim: The vascular endfeet of astrocytes plastered around both arterioles, capillaries and veins in both rodent and human brain express high levels of AQP4 in the membrane facing the vessel wall.
source: Similarly, the vascular endfeet of astrocytes plastered around both arterioles, capillaries and veins in both rodent and human brain express high levels of AQP4 in the membrane facing the vessel wall (Nielsen et al., 1997; Rash et al., 1998; Oberheim et al., 2009; Zeppenfeld et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nielsen et al., 1997; Rash et al., 1998; Oberheim et al., 2009; Zeppenfeld et al., 2017.

claim: The intensity of AQP4 immunofluorescence signal in endfeet plastered around veins is almost double of those surrounding arteries.
source: In fact, the intensity of AQP4 immunofluorescence signal in endfeet plastered around veins is almost double of those surrounding arteries (Iliff et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iliff et al., 2012.

claim: Fibrous astrocytes in white matter tracts are recognized for their high AQP4 expression.
source: Fibrous astrocytes in white matter tracts are also recognized for their high AQP4 expression (Lundgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lundgaard et al., 2014.

claim: AQP4 is present at high density at most if not all glymphatic efflux paths.
source: Thus, AQP4 is present at high density at most if not all glymphatic efflux paths, and therefore also in a prime position to mediate outflow of interstitial fluid.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited literature and experimental data.

claim: CSF distribution is dependent on arousal state and circadian timing rather than being dictated by the rate of CSF production.
source: This is consistent with growing evidence that CSF distribution is dependent on arousal state and circadian timing rather than being dictated by the rate of CSF production (Hablitz et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hablitz et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Vascular density or fast diffusion estimates were not altered by AQP4 deletion.
source: Furthermore, vascular density or fast diffusion estimates were not altered by AQP4 deletion, suggesting that the vasculature and blood perfusion remains the same even after genetic deletion of AQP4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slow MR diffusion measures are increased mostly due to an enlarged interstitial space in AQP4 KO mice.
source: Instead, we show that slow MR diffusion measures are increased mostly due to an enlarged interstitial space.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only slight 5–6% increase in the mean ADC and D might result from superposition of opposing effects of reduced transmembrane permeability (reducing ADC) and increased extracellular space (increasing ADC).
source: Only slight 5–6% increase in the mean ADC and D might result from superposition of opposing effects of reduced transmembrane permeability (reducing ADC) and increased extracellular space (increasing ADC) as concluded previously using time-dependent diffusion MRI and Latour's model of long-time diffusion behavior (Pavlin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citation to Pavlin et al., 2017.

claim: Evaluation of ADC using multi-b-value-multi-diffusion-time DWI provided higher ADC's in healthy hemispheres of mice subjected to contralateral ischemic stroke, reflecting larger interstitial space in AQP4 KO.
source: Similarly, evaluation of ADC using multi-b-value-multi-diffusion-time DWI provided higher ADC's in healthy hemispheres of mice subjected to contralateral ischemic stroke, reflecting larger interstitial space in KO (Urushihata et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Urushihata et al., 2021.

claim: The enlarged interstitial space in both awake and anesthetized AQP4 KO mice is consistent with previous reports under anesthesia.
source: The enlarged interstitial space in both awake and anesthetized AQP4 KO mice is also consistent with previous reports under anesthesia (Yao et al., 2008; Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Papadopoulos et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yao et al., 2008; Amiry-Moghaddam et al., 2003b; Papadopoulos et al., 2004.

claim: Findings in the water phantom filled with Sephadex microbeads confirmed increase in both ADC and D resulting from increased free fluid volume.
source: Our findings in the water phantom filled with Sephadex microbeads of similar porosity but different sizes also confirmed increase in both ADC and D resulting from increased free fluid volume (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cerebrospinal fluid is driven by vascular movement into the brain alongside the perivascular space.
source: Our findings support a glymphatic model whereby cerebrospinal fluid is driven by vascular movement into the brain alongside the perivascular space, and AQP4 at the vascular astrocytic endfoot enables ISF and solute movement from the parenchyma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and established glymphatic model.

claim: AQP4 at the vascular astrocytic endfoot enables ISF and solute movement from the parenchyma.
source: Our findings support a glymphatic model whereby cerebrospinal fluid is driven by vascular movement into the brain alongside the perivascular space, and AQP4 at the vascular astrocytic endfoot enables ISF and solute movement from the parenchyma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and established glymphatic model.

claim: Changes in the micro- and macroscopic CNS fluid compartments could be due to an increased resistance towards glymphatic fluid efflux caused by lack of AQP4 channels along the perivenous space.
source: These changes in the micro- and macroscopic CNS fluid compartments could be due, specifically, an increased resistance towards glymphatic fluid efflux caused by lack of AQP4 channels along the perivenous space (Xie et al., 2013; Plá et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to Xie et al., 2013 and Plá et al., 2022.

claim: Fluid accumulation in the interstitial space would increase resistance toward periarterial CSF influx explaining the overall suppression of glymphatic transport.
source: Fluid accumulation in the interstitial space would, in turn, increase resistance toward periarterial CSF influx explaining the overall suppression of glymphatic transport.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: A meta-analysis of all published studies demonstrated a significant decrease in CSF tracer transport in AQP4 KO mice compared to wildtype.
source: A meta-analysis of all published studies demonstrated a significant decrease in CSF tracer transport in AQP4 KO mice compared to wildtype and meta-regression suggested that differences in anesthesia, age, and tracer delivery explained the opposing results.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a meta-analysis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Meta-regression suggested that differences in anesthesia, age, and tracer delivery explained the opposing results regarding AQP4's role in glymphatic transport.
source: A meta-analysis of all published studies demonstrated a significant decrease in CSF tracer transport in AQP4 KO mice compared to wildtype and meta-regression suggested that differences in anesthesia, age, and tracer delivery explained the opposing results.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a meta-analysis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Glymphatic disruption has been observed in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Glymphatic disruption has been observed in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease (AD; Peng et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2016 and Harrison et al., 2020.

claim: Alterations in MR-DWI have been seen in mild cognitive impairment and symptomatic Alzheimer's disease in humans.
source: In humans, alterations in MR-DWI have been seen in mild cognitive impairment and symptomatic AD (Kantarci et al., 2001; Kantarci et al., 2002; Kulkarni et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kantarci et al., 2001; Kantarci et al., 2002; Kulkarni et al., 2020.

claim: Increased slow MR diffusion is found in Alzheimer's disease patients, compared to those with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls.
source: Interestingly, increased slow MR diffusion is also found in AD patients, compared to those with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls (Bergamino et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bergamino et al., 2020.

claim: Known alterations in AQP4 distribution and abundance in Alzheimer's disease may drive increased interstitial fluid stagnation, decreasing glymphatic function.
source: Perhaps known alterations in AQP4 distribution and abundance in AD (Zeppenfeld et al., 2017; Boespflug et al., 2018; Simon et al., 2018) drive increased interstitial fluid stagnation, decreasing glymphatic function past what is expected in natural aging (Kress et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citations to Zeppenfeld et al., 2017; Boespflug et al., 2018; Simon et al., 2018; Kress et al., 2014.

claim: Regional loss of AQP4 may explain subregion-dependent susceptibility to neurodegeneration by driving local interstitial fluid and protein stagnation increasing the risk of aggregation prone proteins.
source: Extending this speculation, perhaps regional loss of AQP4 may explain subregion-dependent susceptibility to neurodegeneration by driving local interstitial fluid and protein stagnation increasing the risk of aggregation prone proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation.

claim: Diffusion MR is a useful tool to evaluate glymphatic function and may serve as valuable translational biomarker to study glymphatics in human disease.
source: Overall, diffusion MR is a useful tool to evaluate glymphatic function and may serve as valuable translational biomarker to study glymphatics in human disease.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and speculation about future applications.

claim: The glymphatic system is a fluid transport network of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) entering the brain along arterial perivascular spaces, exchanging with interstitial fluid (ISF), ultimately establishing directional clearance of interstitial solutes.
source: The glymphatic system is a fluid transport network of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) entering the brain along arterial perivascular spaces, exchanging with interstitial fluid (ISF), ultimately establishing directional clearance of interstitial solutes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge of the glymphatic system.

claim: CSF transport is facilitated by the expression of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels on the perivascular endfeet of astrocytes.
source: CSF transport is facilitated by the expression of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels on the perivascular endfeet of astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge.

claim: Mice with genetic deletion of AQP4 exhibit abnormalities in the brain structure and molecular water transport.
source: Mice with genetic deletion of AQP4 (AQP4 KO) exhibit abnormalities in the brain structure and molecular water transport.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: AQP4 KO mice had larger interstitial spaces and total brain volumes resulting in higher water content and reduced CSF space volumes.
source: AQP4 KO mice had larger interstitial spaces and total brain volumes resulting in higher water content and reduced CSF space volumes, despite similar CSF production rates and vascular density compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AQP4 KO mice had similar CSF production rates compared to wildtype mice.
source: AQP4 KO mice had larger interstitial spaces and total brain volumes resulting in higher water content and reduced CSF space volumes, despite similar CSF production rates and vascular density compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AQP4 KO mice had similar vascular density compared to wildtype mice.
source: AQP4 KO mice had larger interstitial spaces and total brain volumes resulting in higher water content and reduced CSF space volumes, despite similar CSF production rates and vascular density compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The larger interstitial fluid volume in AQP4 KO mice likely resulted in increased slow but not fast MR diffusion measures.
source: The larger interstitial fluid volume likely resulted in increased slow but not fast MR diffusion measures and coincided with reduced glymphatic influx.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The larger interstitial fluid volume in AQP4 KO mice coincided with reduced glymphatic influx.
source: The larger interstitial fluid volume likely resulted in increased slow but not fast MR diffusion measures and coincided with reduced glymphatic influx.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both ADC and D increased along with the free fluid space volume surrounding the microbeads in the phantom experiment.
source: We found both ADC and D increased along with the free fluid space volume surrounding the microbeads, as expected (Lee et al., 2016), with no difference in IVIM measures between the phantoms with microbeads (Appendix 1—figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Appendix 1—figure 1E, with citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: There was high linear correlation between ADC and D, and T1 relaxation times in the phantom experiment.
source: This was reflected with high linear correlation between ADC and D, and T1 relaxation times (r=0.977, p<0.05) and free fluid volume fractions estimated (r=0.97, p<0.01) using MRI and µCT in all phantoms (Figure 2D-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: There was high linear correlation between ADC and D, and free fluid volume fractions estimated using MRI and µCT in the phantom experiment.
source: This was reflected with high linear correlation between ADC and D, and T1 relaxation times (r=0.977, p<0.05) and free fluid volume fractions estimated (r=0.97, p<0.01) using MRI and µCT in all phantoms (Figure 2D-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: From the cisterna magna, the CSF tracer dispersed via the subarachnoid space cisterns to the Circle of Willis, and then dorsally along the middle cerebral artery into the brain parenchyma and anteriorly toward the olfactory bulb.
source: From the cisterna magna (Figure 3A), the CSF tracer dispersed via the subarachnoid space cisterns to the Circle of Willis, and then dorsally along the middle cerebral artery into the brain parenchyma and anteriorly toward the olfactory bulb (Figure 3B), consistent with the previous reports using fluorescent tracers (Iliff et al., 2012; Mestre et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3A and 3B, with citations to Iliff et al., 2012 and Mestre et al., 2018a.

claim: There were no differences in the tracer distribution within the perivascular space at the basal cistern between AQP4 KO and wildtype mice.
source: Importantly, there were no differences in the tracer distribution within the perivascular space at the basal cistern (Figure 3B – 'Circle of Willis'), consistent with the perivascular space volume not differing between the two genotypes (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3B, Figure 1C, and Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: Differences in tracer signal enhancement were especially visible in the striatum, thalamus, hippocampus, and visual and cingulate/retrosplenial cortex.
source: Differences were especially visible in the striatum (p<0.01), thalamus (p<0.05), hippocampus (p<0.01), and visual and cingulate/retrosplenial cortex (p<0.01 for both; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Within parenchyma, the difference in tracer signal increased with time from infusion and was largest in the cortex and hippocampus.
source: Within parenchyma, the difference increased with time from infusion and was largest in the cortex and hippocampus (p<0.001 at T=80 min; Figure 3C and E, and Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3C, 3E, and Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: The reduced parenchymal influx of contrast agent after cisterna magna injection in AQP4 KO vs. wildtype mice are consistent with current models of glymphatic function.
source: The reduced parenchymal influx of contrast agent after cisterna magna injection in KO vs. WT mice are consistent with current models of glymphatic function (Iliff et al., 2012; Mestre et al., 2018a; Kress et al., 2014; Mestre et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and citations to Iliff et al., 2012; Mestre et al., 2018a; Kress et al., 2014; Mestre et al., 2018b.

claim: The largest delay in the tracer arrival time was visible in the lateral ventricles and caudate nucleus in AQP4 KO mice.
source: The largest delay in the tracer arrival time was visible in the lateral ventricles and caudate nucleus in KO (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Table 3.

claim: Delayed tracer arrival time and time-to-peak, lower peak intensity, and duration of tracer accumulation, as well as smaller area under the DCE curve in AQP4 KO mice indicate a reduced tracer parenchymal influx and higher parenchymal resistance associated with lack of AQP4 channels.
source: Together, delayed tracer arrival time and time-to-peak, lower peak intensity, and duration of tracer accumulation, as well as smaller area under the DCE curve in KO mice indicate a reduced tracer parenchymal influx and higher parenchymal resistance associated with lack of AQP4 channels (Mestre et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to Mestre et al., 2018a.

claim: Vascular density having a low to moderate correlation with arrival time was found in wildtype animals.
source: However, when investigating tracer accumulation dynamics, we found vascular density having a low to moderate correlation with arrival time (Spearman's rho=0.6715, p=0.0201) and moderate to high correlation with time-to-peak in WT animals (rho=0.8411, p=0.0013; Appendix 1—figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Appendix 1—figure 2C.

claim: Vascular density having a moderate to high correlation with time-to-peak was found in wildtype animals.
source: However, when investigating tracer accumulation dynamics, we found vascular density having a low to moderate correlation with arrival time (Spearman's rho=0.6715, p=0.0201) and moderate to high correlation with time-to-peak in WT animals (rho=0.8411, p=0.0013; Appendix 1—figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Appendix 1—figure 2C.

claim: In AQP4 KO animals, only a low range correlation with time-to-peak was identified.
source: In KO animals, only a low range correlation with time-to-peak was identified (rho=0.6084, p=0.0398).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In wildtype mice, AQP4 expression did not correlate with changes in the MR tracer dynamics.
source: Interestingly, in WT mice AQP4 expression did not correlate with changes in the MR tracer dynamics (Appendix 1—figure 2D), but had a moderate linear correlation with both ADC (r=0.77, p=0.0092) and D (r=0.74, p=0.0137; Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and shown in Appendix 1—figure 2D.

claim: Vascular density determines the speed of tracer distribution.
source: These observations suggest that vascular density determines the speed of tracer distribution whereas AQP4 expression determines interstitial fluid exchange.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: AQP4 expression determines interstitial fluid exchange.
source: These observations suggest that vascular density determines the speed of tracer distribution whereas AQP4 expression determines interstitial fluid exchange.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The correlation between slow MR diffusion, ADC and D, with AQP4 density across 10 regions in wildtype mice suggests that AQP4 expression is higher in regions with relatively larger interstitial fluid volume.
source: Also, the correlation between slow MR diffusion, ADC and D, with AQP4 density across 10 regions in WT mice (Figure 2I) suggests that AQP4 expression is higher in regions with relatively larger interstitial fluid volume, possibly reflecting that AQP4 is upregulated in response to stagnation of interstitial fluid in wildtype mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: AQP4 is upregulated in response to stagnation of interstitial fluid in wildtype mice.
source: Also, the correlation between slow MR diffusion, ADC and D, with AQP4 density across 10 regions in WT mice (Figure 2I) suggests that AQP4 expression is higher in regions with relatively larger interstitial fluid volume, possibly reflecting that AQP4 is upregulated in response to stagnation of interstitial fluid in wildtype mice.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Increased AQP4 expression in regions manifesting high ADC or D in wildtype mice may reflect a compensatory upregulation of AQP4 due to fluid stagnation.
source: Increased AQP4 expression in regions manifesting high ADC or D in WTs, possible due enlarged interstitial volume, may reflect a compensatory upregulation of AQP4 due to fluid stagnation consistent with the notion that AQPs reduce parenchymal resistance and facilitate the water and solute movement.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from experimental data.

claim: AQPs reduce parenchymal resistance and facilitate the water and solute movement.
source: Increased AQP4 expression in regions manifesting high ADC or D in WTs, possible due enlarged interstitial volume, may reflect a compensatory upregulation of AQP4 due to fluid stagnation consistent with the notion that AQPs reduce parenchymal resistance and facilitate the water and solute movement.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and inference.

claim: Recent studies report dynamic AQP4 relocalization leading to changes in signaling pathways.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, recent studies report dynamic AQP4 relocalization leading to changes in signaling pathways (Salman et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Salman et al., 2022.
